builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
summary: Robo-SWE replaces ad hoc or general-purpose benchmarks (such as SWE-bench-style tasks) for evaluating coding agents on robotics software, providing 236 executable issue-resolution tasks with containers, developer fixes, and fail-to-pass tests. It costs the effort of building and running per-repository containers at pinned commits and requires execution infrastructure to run tests offline; no model training is needed, but reproducing ROS 2 and physics-engine environments is nontrivial. It can fail as an evaluation proxy because task validity is execution-verified but fairness is not human-reviewed, and the 236-task sample across 28 repositories may not represent a given team's stack, so agent rankings may not transfer.
rationale: The reader operates production coding-agent workflows and can use this benchmark to select or validate agents for robotics code, but only if their domain overlaps; otherwise it is a reference leaderboard to monitor rather than infrastructure to adopt.

claims.statement: Robo-SWE replaces ad hoc or general-purpose benchmarks (such as SWE-bench-style tasks) for evaluating coding agents on robotics software, providing 236 executable issue-resolution tasks with containers, developer fixes, and fail-to-pass tests. It costs the effort of building and running per-repository containers at pinned commits and requires execution infrastructure to run tests offline; no model training is needed, but reproducing ROS 2 and physics-engine environments is nontrivial. It can fail as an evaluation proxy because task validity is execution-verified but fairness is not human-reviewed, and the 236-task sample across 28 repositories may not represent a given team's stack, so agent rankings may not transfer.

Coding agents resolve 43.9%-56.5% of the 236 robotics tasks across setups (Claude Opus 5.5 best at 56.5%), demonstrating measurable differentiation of agent capability on domain-specific robotics issues.
